title: Poisson Summation Sampling and Lattice Duality

items.title: Full-rank lattices, covolume, and the dual lattice
items.statement: Let $n\ge1$. A **full-rank lattice** in $\mathbb R^n$ is a subgroup $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ of the form $\Lambda=A\mathbb Z^n$ for an invertible real $n\times n$ matrix $A$ (equivalently, a full Euclidean lattice in the sense of [[def-full-euclidean-lattice-and-covolume]]; the columns of $A$ are a $\mathbb Z$-basis). Its **covolume** is $\operatorname{covol}(\Lambda):=|\det A|>0$, and its **dual lattice** is $$\Lambda^*:=\{\xi\in\mathbb R^n:\xi\cdot\lambda\in\mathbb Z\text{ for every }\lambda\in\Lambda\}=A^{-T}\mathbb Z^n,\qquad A^{-T}:=(A^{-1})^{T}=(A^{T})^{-1}.$$ Both objects are independent of the chosen matrix: if $B=AU$ with $U\in\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb Z)$, then $|\det B|=|\det A|$ and $B^{-T}\mathbb Z^n=A^{-T}(U^{-T}\mathbb Z^n)=A^{-T}\mathbb Z^n$, because $U^{-T}\in\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb Z)$ preserves $\mathbb Z^n$. The dual $\Lambda^*$ is again a full-rank lattice with $\operatorname{covol}(\Lambda^*)=\operatorname{covol}(\Lambda)^{-1}$, and $\Lambda^*=\mathbb Z^n$ when $\Lambda=\mathbb Z^n$. Moreover $x\mapsto e^{2\pi i\lambda^*\cdot x}$ is $\Lambda$-periodic exactly when $\lambda^*\in\Lambda^*$, so $\Lambda^*$ indexes the lattice characters of the torus $\mathbb R^n/\Lambda$ in the lattice case of [[def-pontryagin-dual-and-compact-open-topology]]. No choice principle is used.

items.strategy: Well-definedness. The two descriptions of $\Lambda$ agree with [[def-full-euclidean-lattice-and-covolume]]: $A$ is the matrix of a $\mathbb Z$-basis, and the covolume is basis-independent by [[thm-determinant-multiplicative]], [[cor-determinant-of-an-inverse]] and $\det U=\pm1$ for $U\in\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb Z)$. Membership: if $\xi=A^{-T}m$ and $\lambda=Ak$, then $\xi\cdot\lambda=m\cdot k\in\mathbb Z$; conversely $\xi\cdot Ak\in\mathbb Z$ for all $k\in\mathbb Z^n$ forces $A^{T}\xi\in\mathbb Z^n$, so $\xi\in A^{-T}\mathbb Z^n$. In particular $A^{-T}\mathbb Z^n$ depends only on $\Lambda$, since replacing $A$ by $AU$ leaves it unchanged. Full rank: the columns of $A^{-T}$ are a real basis ([[thm-real-square-matrix-invertible-iff-determinant-nonzero]]), and $\operatorname{covol}(\Lambda^*)=|\det A^{-T}|=|\det A|^{-1}$. Character clause: for $\lambda^*\in\mathbb R^n$, periodicity of $e^{2\pi i\lambda^*\cdot x}$ under $x\mapsto x+\lambda$ is equivalent to $e^{2\pi i\lambda^*\cdot\lambda}=1$ ([[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]]), i.e. to $\lambda^*\cdot\lambda\in\mathbb Z$. This is a definition item: no proof is supplied beyond this well-definedness check, and it is choice-free.

items.title: Invertible linear substitutions preserve Schwartz space
items.statement: Let $A$ be an invertible real $n\times n$ matrix and put $(A^{*}f)(y):=f(Ay)$. If $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ then $A^{*}f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$; more precisely, for every pair of multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$ there are a constant $C_{\alpha\beta}$ and a finite set of Schwartz seminorms of $f$ with $$p_{\alpha\beta}(A^{*}f)\le C_{\alpha\beta}\max_{|\delta|\le|\alpha|,\,|\gamma|\le|\beta|}p_{\delta\gamma}(f).$$ Hence $f\mapsto f\circ A$ is a continuous linear endomorphism of $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ with continuous inverse $f\mapsto f\circ A^{-1}$. No choice principle is used.

items.strategy: Chain rule. Iterating [[thm-chain-rule]] for the smooth map $y\mapsto Ay$, each derivative is $\partial^{\beta}(f\circ A)(y)=\sum_{|\gamma|=|\beta|}c_{\beta\gamma}(\partial^{\gamma}f)(Ay)$ with constants depending only on $A$. Since $A$ is invertible, $|y|\le\|A^{-1}\||Ay|$ ([[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]], [[thm-real-square-matrix-invertible-iff-determinant-nonzero]]), so $|y^{\alpha}|\le C(1+|Ay|)^{|\alpha|}$; applying [[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]] to the finitely many seminorms $p_{\delta\gamma}(f)$ with $|\delta|\le|\alpha|$ bounds $p_{\alpha\beta}(A^{*}f)$. The same computation with $A^{-1}$ gives the continuous inverse, and all estimates are finite-dimensional and choice-free.

items.title: Fundamental parallelotopes of a lattice tile Euclidean space with covolume volume
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $A$ be an invertible
real $n\times n$ matrix, $\Lambda=A\mathbb Z^n$ a full-rank lattice, and
$$F:=A\bigl((0,1]^n\bigr)=\Bigl\{\sum_{i=1}^n t_i a_i:0<t_i\le1\Bigr\},$$
where $a_1,\dots,a_n$ are the columns of $A$, the fundamental parallelotope of
$\Lambda$. Then every $x\in\mathbb R^n$ has a unique representation
$x=\lambda+p$ with $\lambda\in\Lambda$ and $p\in F$; consequently the translates
$F+\lambda$ ($\lambda\in\Lambda$) are pairwise disjoint and cover
$\mathbb R^n$. Moreover $F$ is Lebesgue measurable and
$\lambda_n(F)=|\det A|=\operatorname{covol}(\Lambda)$. Countable Choice is inherited by the box-measure and linear
change-of-variables suppliers in the volume computation; the unique
representation is choice-free.

references.title: Lior Silberman, Fourier series and the Poisson summation formula (Math 604/613 notes, UBC)
references.locator: §1, Exercises 5-6: the half-open parallelotope and $\{\sum a_iv_i: a\in[0,1)\}$ are fundamental domains; integration over $T=V/\Lambda$ and $\operatorname{vol}(T)=\operatorname{vol}(F)$, PDF pp. 1-2

references.title: Michael E. Taylor, Fourier Analysis, Distributions, and Constant-Coefficient Linear PDE (author PDF)
references.locator: §7, (7.11)-(7.14): the translates of the rectangle $\Omega$ by $\Gamma$ tile $\mathbb R^n$ and the periodisation is formed from them, printed p. 72

items.strategy: Uniqueness. Write $x=Ay$; by [[lem-integer-part]] each coordinate of $y$ has a unique decomposition $y_i=m_i+s_i$ with $m_i\in\mathbb Z$ and $s_i\in(0,1]$. Then $x=Am+As$ with $Am\in\Lambda$ and $As\in F$, and this is the unique such decomposition because $A$ is injective. Disjointness and covering are immediate, and $F$ is the image of the half-open box $(0,1]^n$ under the invertible linear map $A$. Volume: $(0,1]^n$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n((0,1]^n)=1$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]), and $\lambda_n(A(E))=|\det A|\lambda_n(E)$ for measurable $E$ ([[thm-linear-change-of-variables-for-lebesgue-measure]]); this substitution is exactly where Countable Choice enters. The covolume identification is [[def-full-rank-lattice-covolume-and-dual-lattice]].

items.title: Orthogonality of the lattice characters over a fundamental domain
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. Let $A$, $\Lambda= A\mathbb Z^n$ and $F$ be as in [[lem-lattice-fundamental-parallelotope-partitions-euclidean-space]], and let $\lambda^*,\eta^*\in\Lambda^*$. Then $$\frac{1}{\operatorname{covol}(\Lambda)}\int_F e^{2\pi i(\lambda^*-\eta^*)\cdot x}\,dx=\begin{cases}1,&\lambda^*=\eta^*,\\ 0,&\lambda^*\ne\eta^*.\end{cases}$$

references.title: Lior Silberman, Fourier series and the Poisson summation formula (Math 604/613 notes, UBC)
references.locator: §2, Exercise 8: with the Haar probability measure on $T$, $\frac{1}{\operatorname{vol}T}\int_T e(kx)\,dx=\delta_{k,0}$ and $\frac{1}{\operatorname{vol}T}\int_T e(kx)\overline{e(\ell x)}\,dx=\delta_{k\ell}$ for $k,\ell\in\Lambda^*$, PDF p. 3

references.title: Richard S. Laugesen, Harmonic Analysis Lecture Notes (arXiv:0903.3845)
references.locator: ch. 14 and ch. 23 background: characters $e^{2\pi ik\cdot x}$ are orthonormal on the torus, used to expand a periodisation in its Fourier series, PDF pp. 79, 135-138

items.strategy: Put $\mu=\lambda^*-\eta^*$ and substitute $x=Ay$ ([[thm-linear-change-of-variables-for-lebesgue-measure]]): $\int_F e^{2\pi i\mu\cdot x}dx=|\det A|\int_{(0,1]^n}e^{2\pi i(A^{T}\mu)\cdot y}dy$. Since $\mu=\lambda^*-\eta^*\in\Lambda^*$, one has $A^{T}\mu\in\mathbb Z^n$. The integral over the box factorises by [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] into $\prod_{j=1}^n\int_0^1e^{2\pi i(A^{T}\mu)_j y_j}dy_j$, and each one-dimensional factor is $1$ for zero exponent and $0$ otherwise by the exponential primitive ([[lem-complex-integration-by-parts-on-intervals-and-decaying-lines]]); this is the unit-cube case of [[lem-trigonometric-characters-are-orthonormal]]. Finally $A^{T}\mu=0$ if and only if $\mu=0$. Countable Choice is inherited from the substitution interface, as in the volume computation. Apply nonnegative change of variables to the positive and negative real and imaginary parts; boundedness and finite domain volume justify recombination.

items.title: Schwartz periodisation over a lattice is smooth with locally uniformly summable derivatives
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. Let $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ and let $\Lambda$ be a full-rank lattice. Then the periodisation $$P_\Lambda f(x):=\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}f(x+\lambda)$$ converges absolutely for every $x\in\mathbb R^n$, locally uniformly together with the derivative series $\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\partial^{\beta}f(x+\lambda)$ for every multi-index $\beta$; the sum $P_\Lambda f$ is smooth and $\Lambda$-periodic with $\partial^{\beta}(P_\Lambda f)=\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\partial^{\beta}f(x+\lambda)$.

references.title: Lior Silberman, Fourier series and the Poisson summation formula (Math 604/613 notes, UBC)
references.locator: §1, Exercise 4: if $f$ decays faster than $(1+|x|)^{-N}$ for large $N$ then $\Pi_\Lambda f\in C(T)$, and for $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ the periodisation is $C^\infty$, PDF p. 2

items.strategy: Reduce to the unit lattice. Choose a matrix $A$ with $\Lambda=A\mathbb Z^n$ and put $g:=f\circ A\in\mathcal S$ ([[lem-invertible-linear-substitutions-preserve-schwartz-space]]). Then $P_\Lambda f(x)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}g(A^{-1}x+k)=P_{\mathbb Z^n}g(A^{-1}x)$. The published [[thm-poisson-summation-for-schwartz-functions]] states that for a Schwartz function the unit-lattice periodisation converges locally uniformly with every derivative; composing with the diffeomorphism $x\mapsto A^{-1}x$ preserves local uniformity on compact sets, and [[thm-uniform-derivative-limit-on-a-closed-interval]] upgrades the locally uniform derivative series to the derivative identities. $\Lambda$-periodicity of the limit follows by reindexing the absolutely convergent series (replacing $\lambda$ by $\lambda+\lambda_0$). Countable Choice is inherited from the published Schwartz Poisson theorem. Note: the published theorem is consumed here only through its convergence clause.

items.title: Fourier coefficients of a lattice periodisation
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. Let $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$, let $\Lambda$ be a full-rank lattice with dual $\Lambda^*$ and fundamental parallelotope $F$, and let $P:=P_\Lambda f$ be the periodisation of [[lem-schwartz-periodisation-over-a-lattice-is-smooth-and-uniformly-summable]]. Then for every $\lambda^*\in\Lambda^*$, $$\int_F P(x)e^{-2\pi i\lambda^*\cdot x}\,dx=\widehat f(\lambda^*),\qquad\text{so the normalised coefficient is}\qquad \frac{1}{\operatorname{covol}(\Lambda)}\int_F P(x)e^{-2\pi i\lambda^*\cdot x}\,dx=\frac{\widehat f(\lambda^*)}{\operatorname{covol}(\Lambda)},$$ with $\widehat f$ the $L^1$ Fourier transform of [[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]].

references.title: Lior Silberman, Fourier series and the Poisson summation formula (Math 604/613 notes, UBC)
references.locator: §3, Exercise 13(1): $\widehat{\Pi_\Lambda f}(k)=\frac{1}{\operatorname{covol}(\Lambda)}\widehat f(k)$ for $k\in\Lambda^*$, with the normalised Haar measure on $T$, PDF p. 4

references.locator: §7, (7.15)-(7.17): the two expressions for the periodised fundamental solution and the Fourier-series comparison, printed pp. 72-73

items.strategy: Termwise integration. By [[lem-lattice-fundamental-parallelotope-partitions-euclidean-space]] the translates $F+\lambda$ tile $\mathbb R^n$ disjointly; Tonelli ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]) applied to the nonnegative function $(x,\lambda)\mapsto|f(x+\lambda)|$ gives $\sum_{\lambda}\int_F|f(x+\lambda)|dx=\int_{\mathbb R^n}|f|<\infty$, using the translation invariance of Lebesgue measure; hence the series for $P$ may be integrated term by term ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]). In the $\lambda$-th term substitute $y=x+\lambda$ ([[cor-c-one-change-of-variables-for-l-one-functions]]); since $\lambda^*\cdot\lambda\in\mathbb Z$, the exponential factor satisfies $e^{-2\pi i\lambda^*\cdot(y-\lambda)}=e^{-2\pi i\lambda^*\cdot y}$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]]), so the sum over $\lambda$ telescopes to $\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(y)e^{-2\pi i\lambda^*\cdot y}dy=\widehat f(\lambda^*)$.

items.title: The unit-lattice Schwartz Poisson formula is owned by functional analysis (recorded, not proved here)
items.statement: **Recorded, not proved here.** The unit-lattice formula $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}f(k)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)$, together with local uniform convergence of every derivative series of the periodisation $\sum_kf(x+k)$, is the published [[thm-poisson-summation-for-schwartz-functions]] under the negative-sign $2\pi$-normalised convention of this library. This page cites that stable id rather than minting a second proof: the local periodisation lemma below consumes exactly its convergence clause, and the lattice scaling is proved locally on this page; both of those items are independent of this recorded remark.

external_dependency.exact_statement: Elkies, §2, Theorem 2 and its proof (printed pp. 10-11): for any lattice $L\subset\mathbb R^n$ and every Schwartz $f$, $\sum_{x\in L}f(x)=(\operatorname{disc}L)^{-1/2}\sum_{y\in L^*}\widehat f(y)$, where $\widehat f(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x)e^{2\pi i\langle x,y\rangle}d\mu(x)$; the proof periodises $F(z)=\sum_{x\in L}f(x+z)$ and expands it in its Fourier series, (28)-(32). For $L=\mathbb Z^n$ this is $\sum_kf(k)=\sum_k\widehat f(k)$, the statement proved locally by the published library item thm-poisson-summation-for-schwartz-functions in the negative-sign convention.

items.title: Continuous lattice-periodic functions are determined by their lattice Fourier coefficients
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. Let $h:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb C$ be continuous and $\Lambda$-periodic for a full-rank lattice $\Lambda$, with fundamental parallelotope $F$. If $\int_Fh(x)e^{-2\pi i\lambda^*\cdot x}dx=0$ for every $\lambda^*\in\Lambda^*$, then $h=0$ everywhere. Consequently a continuous $\Lambda$-periodic function is determined by the family $\bigl(\int_Fh(x)e^{-2\pi i\lambda^*\cdot x}dx\bigr)_{\lambda^*\in\Lambda^*}$ of its unnormalised lattice Fourier coefficients.

references.title: Lior Silberman, Fourier series and the Poisson summation formula (Math 604/613 notes, UBC)
references.locator: §2, Exercises 7(6) and 9(3): the characters separate points of $T$ and $g\mapsto\check g$ is an isometric isomorphism $L^2(\Lambda^*)\to L^2(T)$; and §3, Exercise 10(3): the direct map is its inverse, PDF pp. 2-3

references.locator: ch. 4 and ch. 23: uniqueness of Fourier coefficients for continuous functions on the torus, PDF pp. 26-30 and 135-136

items.strategy: Pull back to the unit lattice. With $\Lambda=A\mathbb Z^n$, put $h_A(y):=h(Ay)$; it is continuous and $\mathbb Z^n$-periodic. For $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, the change of variables $x=Ay$ ([[cor-c-one-change-of-variables-for-l-one-functions]]) gives $$\widehat{h_A}(k)=\int_{(0,1]^n}h(Ay)e^{-2\pi ik\cdot y}dy=\frac{1}{|\det A|}\int_Fh(x)e^{-2\pi i(A^{-T}k)\cdot x}dx=0,$$ because $k\cdot y=k\cdot A^{-1}x=(A^{-T}k)\cdot x$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]]) and $A^{-T}k\in\Lambda^*$. The published [[lem-periodic-continuous-functions-are-determined-by-their-fourier-coefficients]] (which assumes Countable Choice, inherited here) then gives $h_A=0$, and $y\mapsto Ay$ is onto, so $h=0$. The final sentence restates vanishing of the coefficient family.

items.title: Poisson summation for a full-rank lattice
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. Let $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ and let $\Lambda$ be a full-rank lattice with dual $\Lambda^*$ and covolume $c:=\operatorname{covol}(\Lambda)$. Then both series below converge absolutely and $$\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}f(\lambda)=\frac{1}{c}\sum_{\lambda^*\in\Lambda^*}\widehat f(\lambda^*);$$ more precisely, the periodisation identity $$\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}f(x+\lambda)=\frac{1}{c}\sum_{\lambda^*\in\Lambda^*}\widehat f(\lambda^*)e^{2\pi i\lambda^*\cdot x}$$ holds for every $x\in\mathbb R^n$.

references.locator: §3, Exercise 13: the coefficient identity, the expansion $\Pi_\Lambda f=(1/\operatorname{covol})\sum_{\Lambda^*}\widehat f(k)e(kx)$ and $\sum_{v\in\Lambda}f(v)=(1/\operatorname{vol})\sum_{k\in\Lambda^*}\widehat f(k)$, PDF p. 4

items.strategy: Fourier expansion of the periodisation. By [[lem-schwartz-periodisation-over-a-lattice-is-smooth-and-uniformly-summable]], $P:=P_\Lambda f$ is smooth and $\Lambda$-periodic. Since $\widehat f\in\mathcal S$ ([[thm-fourier-transform-maps-schwartz-space-continuously-to-itself]]) the weight bound ([[lem-schwartz-functions-and-all-derivatives-are-integrable]]) and the elementary lattice count $\#\{\lambda^*\in\Lambda^*:|\lambda^*|\le r\}\le C(1+r)^n$ give $\sum_{\lambda^*}|\widehat f(\lambda^*)|<\infty$. Hence $S(x):=c^{-1}\sum_{\lambda^*}\widehat f(\lambda^*)e^{2\pi i\lambda^*\cdot x}$ converges absolutely uniformly to a continuous $\Lambda$-periodic function. Termwise integration using that absolute convergence gives $\int_FS(x)e^{-2\pi i\eta^*\cdot x}dx=c^{-1}\sum_{\lambda^*}\widehat f(\lambda^*)\int_Fe^{2\pi i(\lambda^*-\eta^*)\cdot x}dx=\widehat f(\eta^*)$ for every $\eta^*\in\Lambda^*$, by [[lem-character-orthogonality-on-a-lattice-fundamental-domain]] and [[thm-dominated-convergence]]. By [[lem-fourier-coefficients-of-lattice-periodisation]] the same integral equals $\widehat f(\eta^*)$ for $P$; hence $P-S$ is continuous, $\Lambda$-periodic and has all lattice Fourier coefficients zero, so [[lem-lattice-periodic-continuous-functions-are-determined-by-their-lattice-fourier-coefficients]] gives $P=S$. Evaluating at $x=0$ yields the lattice-sum identity; absolute convergence on the left is the convergence clause of the periodisation lemma.

items.title: Poisson summation under two-sided polynomial decay
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Lambda$ be a full-rank lattice with covolume $c$ and dual $\Lambda^*$, and let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb C$ be continuous with $\int_{\mathbb R^n}|f|<\infty$ and Fourier transform $\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}dx$. Suppose that for some constants $C>0$ and $\varepsilon>0$, $$|f(x)|\le\frac{C}{(1+|x|)^{n+\varepsilon}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad|\widehat f(\xi)|\le\frac{C}{(1+|\xi|)^{n+\varepsilon}}\qquad(x,\xi\in\mathbb R^n).$$ Then for every $x\in\mathbb R^n$ both series converge absolutely (the left one locally uniformly in $x$) and $$\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}f(x+\lambda)=\frac{1}{c}\sum_{\lambda^*\in\Lambda^*}\widehat f(\lambda^*)e^{2\pi i\lambda^*\cdot x};$$ in particular $\sum_{\lambda}f(\lambda)=c^{-1}\sum_{\lambda^*}\widehat f(\lambda^*)$. This is the non-Schwartz hypothesis promised by the design: continuity and two-sided $(n+\varepsilon)$-decay, with no claim for bare $L^1$ data.

items.strategy: Dyadic-annulus convergence. For a compact set $K$ with $|x|\le R$, choose $j_0$ with $2^j\ge2R$. On $2^j\le|\lambda|<2^{j+1}$, $|f(x+\lambda)|\le C_K2^{-j(n+\varepsilon)}$ uniformly for $x\in K$. Since $\lambda=Ak$ and $|k|\le\|A^{-1}\||\lambda|$, the ball $|\lambda|<2^{j+1}$ contains at most $C2^{jn}$ lattice points, by counting the integer coordinates of $k$; the annulus contribution is $O(2^{-j\varepsilon})$, summable by [[thm-geometric-series]]. The finitely many inner lattice points cause no issue, so the periodisation converges locally uniformly and is continuous. Apply the same dyadic count to $\Lambda^*$ and $\widehat f$; its Fourier series is absolutely and uniformly convergent since each exponential has modulus one. Coefficients: $\int_F\sum_{\lambda}|f(x+\lambda)|dx=\sum_{\lambda}\int_{F+\lambda}|f|=\int|f|<\infty$ by Tonelli ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]) and the tiling of [[lem-lattice-fundamental-parallelotope-partitions-euclidean-space]], so termwise integration is justified ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]); substituting $y=x+\lambda$ as in [[lem-fourier-coefficients-of-lattice-periodisation]] gives $\int_FP(x)e^{-2\pi i\lambda^*\cdot x}dx=\widehat f(\lambda^*)$ for every $\lambda^*\in\Lambda^*$. The dual Fourier series has the same coefficients by [[lem-character-orthogonality-on-a-lattice-fundamental-domain]] and [[thm-dominated-convergence]]. Thus $P-S$ is continuous, $\Lambda$-periodic and has all lattice Fourier coefficients zero, so [[lem-lattice-periodic-continuous-functions-are-determined-by-their-lattice-fourier-coefficients]] gives $P=S$. Evaluation at $x=0$ yields the lattice-sum identity; the two-sided decay hypotheses are those of the source, and [[rem-lone-integrability-alone-does-not-license-pointwise-poisson-summation]] records why bare $L^1$ is insufficient.

items.title: The Dirac comb of a full-rank lattice transforms to the dual comb
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Lambda$ be a full-rank lattice with covolume $c$ and dual $\Lambda^*$. The $\Lambda$-Dirac comb $\operatorname{comb}_\Lambda:=\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\delta_\lambda$, defined by $\langle\operatorname{comb}_\Lambda,\varphi\rangle=\sum_{\lambda}\varphi(\lambda)$, is a tempered distribution, and $$\mathcal F\operatorname{comb}_\Lambda=c^{-1}\operatorname{comb}_{\Lambda^*}\qquad\text{in }\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n),$$ that is, $\langle\mathcal F\operatorname{comb}_\Lambda,\varphi\rangle=c^{-1}\sum_{\lambda^*\in\Lambda^*}\varphi(\lambda^*)$ for every $\varphi\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$. For $\Lambda=\mathbb Z^n$ ($c=1$, $\Lambda^*=\mathbb Z^n$) this is Fourier-invariance of the unit comb, the published [[thm-unit-lattice-dirac-comb-is-fourier-invariant-in-tempered-distributions]]; the scaled case here ($\Lambda=h\mathbb Z^n$, $c=h^n$) is what the sampling lemma below consumes.

references.title: Richard S. Laugesen, Harmonic Analysis Lecture Notes (arXiv:0903.3845)
references.locator: ch. 23, Definition 23.1 and Theorem 23.5: the periodisation identity behind the distributional comb duality, PDF pp. 135-138

references.title: Noam Elkies, Theta functions and weighted theta functions of Euclidean lattices (author PDF)
references.locator: §2, Theorem 2 and the discriminant normalisation (26)-(27): the general-lattice Poisson identity whose unit case is the comb duality, printed pp. 9-11

items.strategy: Temperedness. Choose $L>n$ and use the shell estimate of the unit case ([[def-dirac-comb]]) transported by $\lambda=Ak$: the shell $m\le|\lambda|<m+1$ meets $\Lambda$ in at most $C(1+m)^{n-1}$ points ([[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]), while [[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]] gives $|\varphi(\lambda)|\le A_{n,L}(1+|\lambda|)^{-L}\max_{|\alpha|\le L}p_{\alpha,0}(\varphi)$. The shell series is dominated by a constant times $\sum_mm^{n-1-L}$, which converges ([[thm-p-series-real-exponents]]), so $\operatorname{comb}_\Lambda$ obeys one finite-seminorm estimate and [[thm-finite-seminorm-bound-characterizes-tempered-distributions]] applies; on compactly supported tests the sum is locally finite and agrees with the sum of Dirac distributions [[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]. Transform: for $\varphi\in\mathcal S$, the definition of the tempered transform ([[def-fourier-transform-of-a-tempered-distribution]]) gives $\langle\mathcal F\operatorname{comb}_\Lambda,\varphi\rangle=\sum_{\lambda}\widehat\varphi(\lambda)$. Apply [[thm-poisson-summation-for-a-full-rank-lattice]] to the Schwartz function $\widehat\varphi$: $\sum_{\lambda}\widehat\varphi(\lambda)=c^{-1}\sum_{\lambda^*}\widehat{\widehat\varphi}(\lambda^*)=c^{-1}\sum_{\lambda^*}\varphi(-\lambda^*)$ by $\mathcal F^2=R$ ([[cor-fourier-transform-is-a-topological-automorphism-of-schwartz-space]]), and $\lambda^*\mapsto-\lambda^*$ permutes $\Lambda^*$, so the last sum is $c^{-1}\sum_{\lambda^*}\varphi(\lambda^*)=\langle c^{-1}\operatorname{comb}_{\Lambda^*},\varphi\rangle$. Equality on all Schwartz tests proves the identity. The unit specialization agrees with the published unit-comb theorem, which is recorded as a cross-check rather than used.

items.title: Sampling at a lattice produces periodisation of the spectrum over the dual lattice
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. Let $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ and let $\Lambda$ be a full-rank lattice with covolume $c$ and dual $\Lambda^*$. The product $f\cdot\operatorname{comb}_\Lambda\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ equals the sampled distribution $\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}f(\lambda)\delta_\lambda$, and $$\mathcal F\bigl(f\cdot\operatorname{comb}_\Lambda\bigr)=\frac{1}{c}\sum_{\lambda^*\in\Lambda^*}\widehat f(\cdot-\lambda^*)=\frac{1}{c}\bigl(\operatorname{comb}_{\Lambda^*}*\widehat f\bigr),$$ the **periodisation of the spectrum over the dual lattice with scale** $c^{-1}$. In particular for $\Lambda=h\mathbb Z^n$ ($h>0$) sampling at spacing $h$ gives $\mathcal F\bigl(\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}f(hk)\delta_{hk}\bigr)=h^{-n}\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(\cdot-m/h)$.

references.title: Richard S. Laugesen, Harmonic Analysis Lecture Notes (arXiv:0903.3845)
references.locator: ch. 23, Definition 23.1, Lemma 23.3 and Theorem 23.5: periodisation over the dual lattice and the sampling identity, PDF pp. 135-138

references.title: Andrew Sutherland, MIT 18.785 Lecture 16: The functional equation (course PDF)
references.locator: §16.1, the product-to-convolution and Poisson interface for the Gaussian sampling instance, printed pp. 1-3

items.strategy: Product identity. Multiplication of a tempered distribution by a Schwartz function is transposition, $\langle f\cdot u,\psi\rangle=\langle u,f\psi\rangle$, and it preserves $\mathcal S'$ ([[lem-smooth-polynomially-bounded-multipliers-on-schwartz-space]]). Applied to $u=\operatorname{comb}_\Lambda$ and $\psi\in\mathcal S$ this gives $\langle f\cdot\operatorname{comb}_\Lambda,\psi\rangle=\sum_{\lambda}f(\lambda)\psi(\lambda)=\langle\sum_{\lambda}f(\lambda)\delta_\lambda,\psi\rangle$, the sum being absolutely convergent by the shell estimate for $\operatorname{comb}_\Lambda$; this identifies the product with the sampled distribution. Transform: the product-to-convolution law in [[thm-fourier-transform-converts-allowed-tempered-convolutions-to-products]] gives $\mathcal F(f\cdot u)=\widehat f*(\mathcal Fu)$ (distribution-first convolution), and the comb duality [[lem-dirac-comb-of-a-full-rank-lattice-transforms-to-the-dual-comb]] gives $\mathcal Fu=c^{-1}\operatorname{comb}_{\Lambda^*}$. By [[def-convolution-of-a-tempered-distribution-with-a-schwartz-function]], $(c^{-1}\operatorname{comb}_{\Lambda^*}*\widehat f)(x)=c^{-1}\sum_{\lambda^*}\widehat f(x-\lambda^*)$, which is $c^{-1}\sum_{\lambda^*}\widehat f(\cdot-\lambda^*)$; here $\widehat f\in\mathcal S$ by the Schwartz Fourier theorem. The specialization uses $\operatorname{covol}(h\mathbb Z^n)=h^n$ and $(h\mathbb Z^n)^*=h^{-1}\mathbb Z^n$ ([[def-full-rank-lattice-covolume-and-dual-lattice]]).

items.title: The normalised sinc function
items.statement: The **normalised sinc function** is $\operatorname{sinc}:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$, $$\operatorname{sinc}(t):=\frac{\sin(\pi t)}{\pi t}\quad(t\ne0),\qquad\operatorname{sinc}(0):=1.$$ It is continuous and even, $\operatorname{sinc}(k)=\delta_{k0}$ for every $k\in\mathbb Z$, $|\operatorname{sinc}(t)|\le1$ for all $t$, and $|\operatorname{sinc}(t)|\le1/(\pi|t|)$ for $t\ne0$. This is the normalisation used by the sampling theorem on this page: the reconstruction series is $f(x)=\sum_kf(hk)\operatorname{sinc}(x/h-k)$, and the kernel vanishes at every sampling point except its own. No choice principle is used.

references.title: Richard S. Laugesen, Harmonic Analysis Lecture Notes (arXiv:0903.3845)
references.locator: ch. 22, Theorem 22.3 and Remark 22.4: the kernel $\operatorname{sinc}(\omega x_j-\pi n_j)$ vanishes at the other sampling locations; with the substitution $\omega/\pi=1/h$ this is the normalised sinc $\operatorname{sinc}(x/h-k)$ used here, printed pp. 130-132

references.title: Lior Silberman, Fourier series and the Poisson summation formula (Math 604/613 notes, UBC)
references.locator: §3, Exercise 13 and §4, Exercise 16: the character exponential normalisation $e(z)=e^{2\pi iz}$ behind the $\pi t$ normalisation, PDF pp. 3-5

items.strategy: Well-definedness: at $t=0$ the quotient is read off from the Taylor expansion $\sin(\pi t)=\pi t-\frac{(\pi t)^3}{6}+O(t^5)$, so $\operatorname{sinc}(t)\to1$; continuity elsewhere is the continuity of $\sin$ and of $t\mapsto1/t$ on $t\ne0$ ([[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]], [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]). Evenness is $\sin(-u)=-\sin u$; the integer zeros and $\sin(\pi/2)=1$ are [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]]; the bounds follow from $|\sin u|\le\min(1,|u|)$ applied to $u=\pi t$. This is a definition item; the Fourier transform identity $\operatorname{sinc}(t)=\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}e^{-2\pi it\xi}d\xi$ is not claimed here but is available as the interval indicator example [[ex-fourier-transform-of-an-interval-indicator]] and is consumed by the sampling theorem.

items.title: Band-limited samples are the Fourier coefficients of the rescaled spectrum
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $h>0$ and let
$f\in L^2(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$ have Plancherel transform
$\widehat f:=\mathcal F_2f$ ([[thm-plancherel]]) vanishing almost everywhere off
the band $[-1/(2h),1/(2h)]$. Then $\widehat f\in L^1$, so $f$ has a continuous
representative, again written $f$, with
$$f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R}\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\xi}\,d\xi$$
for every $x$. Choose a measurable representative of $\widehat f$, set
$G_h(\theta):=h^{-1/2}\widehat f(-\theta/h)$ on the half-open interval
$[-1/2,1/2)$, and extend $G_h$ one-periodically to $\mathbb R$. Its
almost-everywhere class is independent of the chosen representative and defines
a function class on the circle $\mathbb T=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]]). Then
$G_h\in L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$, and for every $k\in\mathbb Z$ its $k$-th
Fourier coefficient ([[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]])
is
$$\widehat{G_h}(k)=h^{1/2}f(hk).$$
Consequently $\bigl(h^{1/2}f(hk)\bigr)_{k\in\mathbb Z}\in\ell^2(\mathbb Z)$ and
$$\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}|f(hk)|^2=h^{-1}\|f\|_{L^2(\mathbb R)}^2 .$$
The reflection $\theta\mapsto-\theta$ in the definition of $G_h$ is inserted
only so that the library's negative-sign coefficient convention matches the
samples $f(hk)$ rather than $f(-hk)$.

references.title: Richard S. Laugesen, Harmonic Analysis Lecture Notes (arXiv:0903.3845)
references.locator: ch. 22, proof of Theorem 22.3, (22.1)-(22.2): after rescaling $\omega=\pi$ the coefficients of $\widehat f$ on the cube are the samples $f(-n)$, then reindexed to $f(n)$; the sampling map is the Fourier coefficient map of the band, printed pp. 131-133

references.title: Lior Silberman, Fourier series and the Poisson summation formula (Math 604/613 notes, UBC)
references.locator: §2, Exercises 8-9 and §3, Exercise 13: the characters $e_k$, the isometric isomorphism $L^2(\Lambda^*)\to L^2(T)$ (Parseval) and the coefficient identity, PDF pp. 2-4

items.strategy: Continuous representative. $\widehat f$ is square-integrable and supported in a set of finite Lebesgue measure, so $\widehat f\in L^1$ ([[thm-finite-measure-l-r-includes-into-l-p-for-p-less-r]] applied on the band). The integral $g(x):=\int\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\xi}d\xi$ is bounded and continuous ([[thm-fourier-transform-maps-l-one-to-bounded-uniformly-continuous-functions]]); on $L^1\cap L^2$ the integral transform agrees with the $L^2$ transform ([[thm-l-one-l-two-agreement-of-fourier-transform]]), and $\mathcal F_2\widehat f=Rf$ ([[thm-l-two-fourier-inversion]]), so $g=Rf$ almost everywhere and $f$ is represented everywhere by $x\mapsto g(-x)=\int\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\xi}d\xi$. Coefficients. Substituting $\theta=-h\xi$ ([[cor-c-one-change-of-variables-for-l-one-functions]]) in $\widehat{G_h}(k)=\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}G_h(\theta)e^{-2\pi ik\theta}d\theta$ gives $h^{-1/2}\cdot h\int\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ikh\xi}d\xi=h^{1/2}f(hk)$, using the representative formula. Square summability. $\|G_h\|^2_{L^2(\mathbb T)}=h^{-1}\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}|\widehat f(-\theta/h)|^2d\theta=\|\widehat f\|_{L^2}^2=\|f\|_{L^2}^2$, and the isometry clause of [[thm-riesz-fischer-for-fourier-coefficients]] gives $\sum_k|\widehat{G_h}(k)|^2=\|G_h\|^2$; substituting $\widehat{G_h}(k)=h^{1/2}f(hk)$ yields $\sum_k|f(hk)|^2=h^{-1}\|f\|^2$. Countable choice is inherited from the Euclidean integration and Fourier interfaces named above.

items.title: Shannon sampling for band-limited $L^2$ functions
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. Let $h>0$ and let $f\in L^2(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$ have $L^2$ Fourier transform vanishing almost everywhere off the band $[-1/(2h),1/(2h)]$; write $f$ also for its continuous representative. Then $$f(x)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}f(hk)\operatorname{sinc}(x/h-k)\qquad\text{with convergence in }L^2(\mathbb R).$$ If in addition $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}|f(hk)|<\infty$, then the series converges absolutely and uniformly on every compact subset of $\mathbb R$, its sum is continuous, and the identity holds for every $x\in\mathbb R$. In the $L^2$-only case no pointwise convergence and no evaluation at a non-Lebesgue representative value is claimed.

references.title: Richard S. Laugesen, Harmonic Analysis Lecture Notes (arXiv:0903.3845)
references.locator: ch. 22, Theorem 22.3 and its proof, printed pp. 130-133: expansion of the band-limited spectrum in the coefficients $f((\pi/\omega)n)$, inverse transform of the modulated indicator, and the sinc series; Remark 22.4(2) records that the kernel vanishes at the other samples

references.title: Lior Silberman, Fourier series and the Poisson summation formula (Math 604/613 notes, UBC)
references.locator: §2-§3, Exercises 9-10 and 13: the $L^2$ Fourier series expansion on $T$ is an isometric isomorphism and the coefficients are the band samples, PDF pp. 3-4

items.strategy: $L^2$ identity. By [[lem-bandlimited-samples-are-fourier-coefficients-on-the-band-interval]], $G_h(\theta)=h^{-1/2}\widehat f(-\theta/h)$ has coefficients $\widehat{G_h}(k)=h^{1/2}f(hk)$ and lies in $L^2(\mathbb T)$; the expansion clause of [[thm-riesz-fischer-for-fourier-coefficients]] gives $G_h=\sum_k\widehat{G_h}(k)e_k$ in $L^2(\mathbb T)$. Rescaling back, $\widehat f(\xi)=h\sum_kf(hk)e^{-2\pi ihk\xi}$ on the band (and $0$ off it), as an $L^2(\mathbb R)$ identity. Apply the unitary inverse transform ([[thm-plancherel]], [[thm-l-two-fourier-inversion]]) term by term: each term is the inverse transform of the modulated interval indicator, and the complex FTC ([[lem-complex-integration-by-parts-on-intervals-and-decaying-lines]], [[ex-fourier-transform-of-an-interval-indicator]]) computes $\int_{-1/(2h)}^{1/(2h)}e^{2\pi i(x-hk)\xi}d\xi=\frac1h\operatorname{sinc}(x/h-k)$ with the normalisation of [[def-normalized-sinc-function]]. Multiplying by the coefficient $h\,f(hk)$ yields the term $f(hk)\operatorname{sinc}(x/h-k)$, and unitarity transfers the $L^2$ convergence of the series to $L^2(\mathbb R)$. Local uniformity. Under $\sum_k|f(hk)|<\infty$, the bounds $|\operatorname{sinc}(t)|\le1$ and $|\operatorname{sinc}(t)|\le1/(\pi|t|)$ of [[def-normalized-sinc-function]] give, on $|x|\le R$, $\sum_k|f(hk)|\,|\operatorname{sinc}(x/h-k)|\le C_R\sum_k|f(hk)|<\infty$ with a constant $C_R$ depending only on $h,R$. Weierstrass gives absolute and locally uniform convergence; the continuous sum agrees with the $L^2$ class of $f$ almost everywhere, and two continuous functions equal almost everywhere are equal everywhere. No pointwise claim is made without the extra hypothesis.

items.title: The Nyquist no-aliasing condition
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).
Let $h>0$ and let $E\subseteq\mathbb R$ be Lebesgue measurable which, up to a
Lebesgue null set, is contained in an interval of length $1/h$ (for instance
$\lambda_1\bigl(E\setminus[-1/(2h),1/(2h)]\bigr)=0$). Then the reciprocal
translates $E+m/h$ ($m\in\mathbb Z$) are pairwise disjoint up to null sets:
$\lambda_1\bigl((E+m/h)\cap(E+n/h)\bigr)=0$ for $m\ne n$. Consequently, if $f\in L^2(\mathbb R)$ has Plancherel transform
$\widehat f$ vanishing almost everywhere off $E$, then for almost every $\xi$
at most one term of $Q(\xi):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z}\widehat f(\xi-m/h)$ is nonzero,
and $Q(\xi)=\widehat f(\xi)$ for almost every $\xi\in E$. These assertions are
independent of the measurable representative of $\widehat f$.
For Schwartz $f$, [[lem-sampling-produces-periodisation-in-frequency]]
identifies $h^{-1}Q$ with the Fourier transform of the sampled distribution;
the corollary does not extend that lemma's distributional identity to arbitrary
$L^2$ inputs. If $E$ is essentially contained in the centered band
$[-1/(2h),1/(2h)]$, [[thm-shannon-sampling-for-bandlimited-ltwo-functions]]
also gives the stated reconstruction. A general translated interval of length
$1/h$ has the same no-overlap property, but is not itself that centered-band
hypothesis.

references.title: Richard S. Laugesen, Harmonic Analysis Lecture Notes (arXiv:0903.3845)
references.locator: ch. 22, Theorem 22.3 and Remark 22.4(1): centered-band sampling at spacing proportional to reciprocal bandwidth, printed p. 131; the measurable translate-disjointness assertion is proved locally

references.title: Lior Silberman, Fourier series and the Poisson summation formula (Math 604/613 notes, UBC)
references.locator: §1, Exercise 2 and §2, Exercise 7(1)-(2): the dual lattice and its periodic exponential characters, PDF pp. 1-2; the no-overlap conclusion is proved locally

items.strategy: Measure-theoretic disjointness. Write $E\subseteq I\cup N$ with $I$ an interval of length $1/h$ and $\lambda_1(N)=0$. If $x\in(E+m/h)\cap(E+n/h)$ with $m\ne n$, then $x-m/h$ and $x-n/h$ lie in $E$, hence each lies either in $I$ or in the null set $N$. The intersection is contained in $\bigl((I+m/h)\cap(I+n/h)\bigr)\cup(N+m/h)\cup(N+n/h)$: the first set is empty (two intervals of length $1/h$ whose positions differ by $|n-m|/h\ge1/h$ meet at most in a common endpoint) and the last two are translates of a null set, hence null by [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-and-measurability-are-translation-invariant]]. Conclusion: for almost every $\xi$, the sets $\xi-m/h$ ($m\in\mathbb Z$) cannot meet $E$ in two different translates, so at most one term $\widehat f(\xi-m/h)$ is nonzero. The link to [[lem-sampling-produces-periodisation-in-frequency]] is that the transformed sampled distribution there is exactly the periodisation $h^{-1}\sum_m\widehat f(\cdot-m/h)$ over the dual lattice; a.e. single-term support, with endpoint coincidences discarded as a null set, is the no-aliasing (Nyquist) condition.

items.title: Aliasing when spectral support has positive-measure overlap with a reciprocal translate
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $h>0$ and let
$E\subseteq\mathbb R$ be Lebesgue measurable. Positive-measure overlap
$E\cap(E+m/h)$ for some $m\in\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$ gives a nonzero $L^2$
signal supported spectrally in $E$ whose samples on $h\mathbb Z$ all vanish.
This is the failure mechanism behind reciprocal-lattice periodisation in
[[lem-sampling-produces-periodisation-in-frequency]].

To see this, partition $\mathbb R$ into half-open intervals of length
$|m|/(2h)$. Since the overlap has positive measure, countable subadditivity
([[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]]) gives one interval
$J$ for which $D:=J\cap E\cap(E+m/h)$ has positive measure. It has finite
measure by the box formula ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]),
and $D$ and $D-m/h$ are disjoint because $J$ is shorter than $|m|/h$.
Therefore $g:=\mathbf 1_D-\mathbf 1_{D-m/h}$ is a nonzero $L^1\cap L^2$
function vanishing off $E$. Its inverse Plancherel transform $f$ is nonzero
([[thm-plancherel]]) and has the continuous representative
$f(x)=\int g(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\xi}d\xi$
([[thm-l-two-fourier-inversion]], [[thm-l-one-l-two-agreement-of-fourier-transform]],
[[thm-fourier-transform-maps-l-one-to-bounded-uniformly-continuous-functions]]).
Translation substitution ([[cor-c-one-change-of-variables-for-l-one-functions]])
and the exponential addition and kernel laws
([[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]],
[[thm-kernel-and-fibres-of-complex-exponential]]) give
$f(hk)=(1-e^{-2\pi imk})\int_D e^{2\pi ihk\xi}d\xi=0$ for every integer $k$.
Thus $f$ and the zero signal have identical samples. No extension of the
Schwartz-only distributional sampling formula is needed for this witness.

In the classical interval-band case, an interval of length greater than $1/h$
has positive-measure overlap with its shift by $1/h$. This corresponds to
bandwidth beyond the cutoff $1/(2h)$ at fixed sampling spacing, rather than
a sampling rate above the Nyquist requirement. Being too wide to fit in an
interval of length $1/h$ is insufficient by itself for disconnected $E$:
when $h=1$, the set $E=(0,1/10)\cup(11/10,6/5)$ does not fit essentially in
such an interval, but its fractional parts lie in the disjoint intervals
$(0,1/10)$ and $(1/10,1/5)$. Within each interval the fractional-part map is
injective, so no distinct points of $E$ differ by an integer. Its integer
translates are therefore pairwise disjoint. The centered-band reconstruction
and its convergence modes remain those of
[[thm-shannon-sampling-for-bandlimited-ltwo-functions]].

items.title: Dual lattice and covolume for a diagonal scaling
items.statement: Let $a_1,\dots,a_n\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$ and let $A=\operatorname{diag}(a_1,\dots,a_n)$. For $\Lambda=A\mathbb Z^n$ the covolume is $\operatorname{covol}(\Lambda)=\prod_{i=1}^n|a_i|$ and the dual lattice is $$\Lambda^*=\operatorname{diag}(a_1^{-1},\dots,a_n^{-1})\mathbb Z^n=\Bigl\{\Bigl(\frac{m_1}{a_1},\dots,\frac{m_n}{a_n}\Bigr):m\in\mathbb Z^n\Bigr\},$$ since $A^{-T}=A^{-1}$ for a diagonal matrix. In one dimension, $\operatorname{covol}(a\mathbb Z)=|a|$ and $(a\mathbb Z)^*=a^{-1}\mathbb Z$; for the sampling spacing $a=h>0$ this is the pair $h\mathbb Z$ and $h^{-1}\mathbb Z$ of the sampling results on this pair.

items.title: Shannon reconstruction of a sinc function
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice and let $\operatorname{sinc}$ be the normalised sinc of [[def-normalized-sinc-function]]. Then $\widehat{\operatorname{sinc}}=\mathbf 1_{[-1/2,1/2]}$ as $L^2$ Fourier transforms, so $\operatorname{sinc}$ is band-limited with $h=1$ and band $[-1/2,1/2]$; its samples are $\operatorname{sinc}(k)=\delta_{k0}$; and the Shannon series of [[thm-shannon-sampling-for-bandlimited-ltwo-functions]] for this $f$ is $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\operatorname{sinc}(k)\operatorname{sinc}(x-k)=\operatorname{sinc}(x)$, a single nonzero term at $k=0$ reproducing the function at every $x$. Since $\sum_k|\operatorname{sinc}(k)|=1<\infty$, the locally uniform clause of the theorem applies as well. The example checks the signs, the band endpoints $\pm1/2$ and the $h^{1/2}$ normalisation of the pair.

items.strategy: $L^2$ band limit. The indicator $\mathbf 1_{[-1/2,1/2]}$ lies in $L^1\cap L^2$ and [[ex-fourier-transform-of-an-interval-indicator]] gives its $L^1$ transform as $\sin(\pi t)/(\pi t)=\operatorname{sinc}(t)$; by [[thm-l-one-l-two-agreement-of-fourier-transform]] this is its $L^2$ transform. Then $\mathcal F_2\operatorname{sinc}=\mathcal F_2^2\mathbf 1_{[-1/2,1/2]}=R\mathbf 1_{[-1/2,1/2]}=\mathbf 1_{[-1/2,1/2]}$ ([[thm-l-two-fourier-inversion]]), and $\operatorname{sinc}\in L^2$ because $|\operatorname{sinc}(t)|\le\min(1,1/(\pi|t|))$ ([[def-normalized-sinc-function]]). Hence the band-limited hypothesis with $h=1$ holds. Samples: $\operatorname{sinc}(0)=1$ and $\operatorname{sinc}(k)=0$ for nonzero integers $k$. The reconstruction series collapses to the $k=0$ term. All steps are the published interval-indicator and $L^2$-inversion interfaces; Countable Choice is inherited. This is an example and a leaf.

items.title: Bare $L^1$ data do not license pointwise Poisson summation (recorded)
items.statement:
**Recorded, not proved here.** Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]),
as in the cited midpoint-convergence theorem. The two-sided decay hypotheses of
[[thm-poisson-summation-under-two-sided-polynomial-decay]] cannot be dropped to
bare $L^1$: the periodisation of an $L^1$ function is defined only almost
everywhere and depends pointwise on the chosen representative. A
piecewise $C^1$ periodisation can have jumps where its Fourier series tends to
the midpoint of the one-sided limits instead of its assigned value. Half-open
lattice cells themselves are disjoint; the discrepancy is not double-counting
by the tiling. Concretely,
Laugesen's Example 23.2 periodises $f=\mathbf 1_{[-\pi,2\pi)}$ and finds
$\operatorname{Pe}(f)(x)=2\pi\bigl(2\cdot\mathbf 1_{[-\pi,0)}(x)+\mathbf 1_{[0,\pi)}(x)\bigr)$
for $x\in[-\pi,\pi)$, which is discontinuous at the lattice point $x=0$: its
one-sided limits there are $4\pi$ and $2\pi$, so after rescaling the period to
$1$ its Fourier series converges at $0$ to the midpoint $3\pi$
([[cor-piecewise-c-one-fourier-series-converges-to-midpoint-values]]) rather
than to the value $2\pi$ taken by the periodisation sum at $0$. So a
point-sampled formula $\sum_\lambda f(\lambda)=c^{-1}\sum_{\lambda^*}\widehat f(\lambda^*)$
is not a theorem of bare $L^1$. This example shows the need for additional
pointwise regularity or summability; it does not make the particular polynomial
decay bounds necessary for every function satisfying a Poisson identity. This is a recorded source warning and is not proved on this page.

external_dependency.exact_statement: Laugesen, ch. 23, Example 23.2: "In 1 dimension, if $f=\mathbf 1_{[-\pi,2\pi)}$, then $\operatorname{Pe}(f)=2\pi(2\cdot\mathbf 1_{[-\pi,0)}+\mathbf 1_{[0,\pi)})$ for $x\in[-\pi,\pi)$, with $\operatorname{Pe}(f)$ extending $2\pi$-periodically to $\mathbb R$." Laugesen's Theorem 23.5 then proves the pointwise periodisation identity only under the two-sided decay hypotheses (23.1)-(23.2).

items.title: Distinct pure frequencies differing by a reciprocal-lattice shift have identical samples
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. Let $h>0$, $\xi\in\mathbb R$ and $m\in\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$, and put $f_1(x)=e^{2\pi i\xi x}$ and $f_2(x)=e^{2\pi i(\xi+m/h)x}$. The two functions are distinct, but they agree at every sample of the lattice $h\mathbb Z$: $$f_2(hk)=e^{2\pi i(\xi+m/h)hk}=e^{2\pi i\xi hk}\,e^{2\pi imk}=f_1(hk)\qquad(k\in\mathbb Z),$$ because $mk\in\mathbb Z$ and $e^{2\pi imk}=1$. Hence no procedure reading only the samples on $h\mathbb Z$ can distinguish these two pure frequencies: undersampling shifts the frequency $\xi+m/h$ onto $\xi$, the aliasing mechanism recorded on the companion A page. The witness concerns pure frequencies, which are bounded but not in $L^2(\mathbb R)$; it does not contradict the $L^2$ reconstruction theorem.

Distinctness: the quotient $f_2(x)/f_1(x)=e^{2\pi i(m/h)x}$ equals $-1$ at $x=h/(2m)$, so the functions are not equal. This is a finite computation and a leaf of the B page.
